contract.note: "On the order of" signals a rough magnitude. A figure of $1.2T is the same order of magnitude, so reading the claim as roughly $500B or more is ordinary rather than stretched. The result does depend on that reading, since a strict point estimate would make it an understatement.

evidence.note: Same-day Yahoo Finance screen: chip stocks alone lost about $1.2T on June 5, intraday. That clears the roughly half-trillion threshold even before counting the rest of tech.
CNBC close for June 5: Nasdaq down 4.18%, its worst day since April 2025. This confirms a large tech selloff at the close and matches the Dow figure Marcus cites.

reviews.rationale: Same-day reporting shows chip stocks alone lost about $1.2T intraday on June 5, 2026, and the Nasdaq closed down 4.18%. Tech losses were at least on the order of half a trillion. The only weakness is that his figure understates the loss, which is consistent with a rough magnitude estimate. Note that the screen is intraday and covers chips only.

semantics.note: An unhedged description of SpaceX's present strategy. The "whether making money or losing" clause only sets profitability aside, and the proposition keeps the "by arming competitors" mechanism.

contract.note: Reading "waving the towel" as giving up on competing for frontier models is the ordinary meaning of the idiom. The result turns on that reading, because the leasing itself is not disputed.

evidence.note: TechCrunch, May 20, on SpaceX's IPO filing: plans for a next-generation model with multiple trillions of parameters, and compute owned in order to train frontier models. This is active frontier ambition shortly before the post.

Tom's Hardware, May 15: core training had moved to Colossus 2, and the older Colossus 1 was the cluster leased out. Leasing older capacity while still training matches the contract's contradiction condition.
The article speculates that SpaceX could be positioning itself as a cloud provider. This is only a possibility and does not show that frontier work stopped.
August 2026 release of Grok 4.6, roughly level with rival flagship models. It falls after the target period but is consistent with SpaceX still competing.

reviews.rationale: Reporting from around the post date shows SpaceX/xAI still planning a much larger next-generation frontier model and training on its newer Colossus 2 cluster while leasing out older capacity. That matches the contract's contradiction condition. Later flagship releases fit the same picture. One gap: the evidence predates the June 5 Google lease, but nothing shows that training stopped.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps both "so far" and "many people." The promise of a future post is not the claim; the embedded observation is.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: measured AI productivity gains so far are small, against prominent expectations of large gains. The contract flags that most forecasts run over a 10-year horizon.

evidence.note: Survey of nearly 6,000 executives, Nov 2025–Jan 2026: 89% report no effect of AI on labor productivity, and executives expect much larger effects ahead.
Penn Wharton estimates AI added only about 0.01pp to TFP growth in 2025, which it calls small today.
Goldman Sachs's 2023 forecast of a 1.5pp lift to productivity growth. It shows prominent large expectations, but over a 10-year horizon.
A later Summer 2026 survey wave again finds a modest 0.2% effect. It is dated after the post, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: Independent studies up to mid-2026 find very small measured productivity effects from AI: most firms report none, and the macro estimate is about 0.01pp. Prominent forecasts and executives' own expectations pointed to much larger gains. Some of those forecasts run over 10 years, which weakens the comparison, but the claim still holds on the plain reading.

Under policy, the claim is not scored while the antecedent is unknown. No deadline was given, and no conclusive event exists.
